titulo.en: Martina's voseo: vos sos, vos tenés, vení

objetivo.en: Recognize Martina's voseo (vos sos, tenés, querés, vení) when you hear it and translate it mentally into tú forms.

traduccion.en: the voseo (using vos instead of tú)

nota.en: Say “boh-SEH-oh”: v sounds like a b and every vowel is short and pure. El voseo is the use of vos, and its verb forms, instead of tú.

traduccion.en: vos (an informal “you”, used instead of tú)

nota.en: Say “bohs”: v sounds like a b and the o is short and pure, with no “ou” glide. In Argentina and Uruguay vos is the everyday word for one person you know well.

traduccion.en: from the River Plate region (Argentina and Uruguay)

nota.en: Say “ree-oh-plah-TEHN-seh”. It has one form for both genders: el español rioplatense, una tonada rioplatense. The River Plate (Río de la Plata) lies between Argentina and Uruguay.

traduccion.en: you have (vos form of tener)

nota.en: Say “teh-NEHS”: the stress falls on the last syllable. Tú tienes becomes vos tenés: the stem loses the ie and the ending is stressed.

traduccion.en: you want (vos form of querer)

nota.en: Say “keh-REHS”: qu sounds like a k, the single r is like the tt in American “butter” and the stress falls on the last syllable. Tú quieres becomes vos querés.

traduccion.en: come! (vos command of venir)

nota.en: Say “beh-NEE”: v sounds like a b and the stress falls on the last syllable. The tú command is ven; the vos command drops the final r of the infinitive and stresses the last vowel.

traduccion.en: the woman from Buenos Aires

nota.en: Say “pohr-TEH-nyah”: ñ sounds like the ny in “canyon”. The masculine is el porteño. The word comes from puerto (port), because Buenos Aires is a port city.

traduccion.en: the form of address

nota.en: Say “FOHR-mah deh trah-tah-MYEHN-toh”. It is the way you address a person: tú, usted or vos. Tratar de usted means “to address as usted”.

traduccion.en: the lilt, the regional accent

nota.en: Say “toh-NAH-dah”: the d between vowels is soft, like the th in “this”. La tonada is the melody and rhythm of a region's speech: la tonada rioplatense.

explicacion.en: In English “you” is always the same, so learners mix the pronoun vos with the tú ending. Vos goes with its own forms: vos tenés. The same happens with ser: vos sos, not vos eres.
Learners copy the vos ending to several people. Voseo is only for one person; for two or more, every Latin American says ustedes + tienen.
Ser is the only vos verb that does not simply drop the r: vos sos. Learners often keep the tú form eres after vos.

titulo.en: Three ways to say “you” to one person

texto.en: Spanish has three ways of addressing one person: tú (informal), usted (formal) and vos. Vos is the informal “you” in Argentina and Uruguay and in parts of Central America and Colombia. This is the voseo: vos replaces tú, and the verb changes with it. Usted and ustedes stay the same everywhere; for several people, Latin America says ustedes and only Spain says vosotros. In this course you do not have to use the voseo: you have to recognize it, because Martina, your classmate from Buenos Aires, uses it, and it can appear in the DELE C1.

titulo.en: How the voseo works

texto.en: Present tense: take the infinitive, drop the final r and stress the last vowel: hablar → hablás, tener → tenés, vivir → vivís. The vos form has no stem change (tú tienes, tú quieres, tú puedes become vos tenés, vos querés, vos podés), and ser is irregular: vos sos. Commands: venir → vení, mirar → mirá, andar → andá; pronouns attach at the end: decime (tell me), sentate (sit down). In the other tenses vos uses the same forms as tú. So the method is simple: when you hear vos, translate it in your head to tú: vos tenés = tú tienes, vení = ven.

titulo.en: Tú, vos and usted: the present

texto.en: One person, three ways of addressing them. Read each row from left to right; ser is the only irregular verb in the vos column.

titulo.en: Tú, vos and usted: the command

texto.en: The vos command is the infinitive without the final r, with the stress on the last vowel. Pronouns attach to the end: decime, sentate, escribila.

traduccion.en: You are from Buenos Aires, aren't you?

nota.en: Vos sos = tú eres. Sos is the only irregular vos form.

traduccion.en: Do you have time now?

nota.en: Tenés = tienes. The stem keeps the e and the stress moves to the ending.

traduccion.en: Do you want a coffee?

nota.en: Querés = quieres. As with tú, you can drop the pronoun.

traduccion.en: Look, you speak Spanish very well.

nota.en: Mirá = mira; hablás = hablas. The stress falls on the last syllable.

traduccion.en: Where do you live?

nota.en: Vivís = vives.

traduccion.en: Come on, sit down here for a moment.

nota.en: Vení = ven; sentate = siéntate (sentá + te). Acá is another way to say aquí.

traduccion.en: Tell me what you want to drink.

nota.en: Decime = dime (decí + me).

traduccion.en: Do you all want a coffee?

nota.en: For several people the word is ustedes + quieren, in Argentina too. Voseo is only for one person.

titulo.en: How to hear the voseo

texto.en: To turn a vos form into a tú form, bring back the stem change or the tú ending.

nota.en: -ar: drop the r and stress the á (tú: hablas)
-er: drop the r and stress the é, with no ie (tú: tienes)
-ir: drop the r and stress the í (tú: vives)
command: drop the r and stress the last vowel (tú: ven)

traduccion.en: You speak Spanish.

nota.en: Tú hablas español.

traduccion.en: You are right.

nota.en: Tú tienes razón.

traduccion.en: Come to my house.

nota.en: Ven a mi casa.

consigna.en: Match each voseo form with its tú form.

feedback.en: Vos sos = tú eres, vos tenés = tú tienes, vos querés = tú quieres. Sos is irregular; tenés and querés have no ie and put the stress on the last syllable.

pista.en: Ser is irregular in every column: eres, sos, es. For the others, bring back the ie.

consigna.en: Choose the voseo form that corresponds to «tú tienes».

feedback.en: Vos tenés: the stem keeps the e and the stress falls on the last syllable. Vos tienes mixes vos with the tú form, and vos tengas is a subjunctive.

pista.en: Look at the table: the vos ending is stressed.

consigna.en: Choose the tú command that corresponds to the voseo «vení».

feedback.en: Vení = ven. Vienes is a present tense and vengas is a subjunctive.

pista.en: The tú command of venir is the short form.

consigna.en: Listen and choose what Martina is doing.

feedback.en: ¿Querés un café? is an offer: querés is the vos form of querer, so she asks whether the other person wants one.

consigna.en: Put the pieces in order to write the tú version of «Vos tenés tiempo».

feedback.en: Tú tienes tiempo: the tú form is tienes, with the diphthong ie.

consigna.en: Rewrite in tú: «Vos sos de Buenos Aires.»

feedback.en: Vos sos becomes tú eres. Sos is the vos form of ser; the tú form is eres.

contexto.en: Thursday, March 17, 2033, at the Instituto Andino de Idiomas in Quito. It is the first class of the varieties module of the DELE C1 preparation course, which began on Monday, January 10. Emma García and Martina, a classmate from Buenos Aires, have been classmates since January and use tú with each other (Martina speaks with voseo, Emma answers with tú). Both use usted with the Profesora, who asks Martina to explain the voseo to the group.

dialogo.texto: Buenas tardes a todos. Hoy empezamos el módulo de variedades del curso de preparación para el DELE C1. En el examen van a escuchar a hablantes de varias regiones, y en este grupo tenemos una voz rioplatense. Martina, ¿puede explicar al grupo qué es el voseo?

traduccion.en: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we start the varieties module of the DELE C1 preparation course. In the exam you are going to hear speakers from several regions, and in this group we have a River Plate voice. Martina, can you explain to the group what the voseo is?

dialogo.texto: Con gusto, profesora. Soy de Buenos Aires, soy porteña, aunque mi abuela era de Rosario. Vivo en Quito desde hace unos meses. En Argentina y en otras zonas usamos vos en lugar de tú. Para mí es lo más natural: vos sos, vos tenés, vos querés, vos vivís. Es una forma de tratamiento y es muy común. En mi casa, todos hablamos así.

traduccion.en: Gladly, teacher. I'm from Buenos Aires, I'm a porteña, although my grandmother was from Rosario. I have lived in Quito for a few months. In Argentina and in other areas we use vos instead of tú. For me it is the most natural thing: vos sos, vos tenés, vos querés, vos vivís. It is a form of address and it is very common. At my house, everyone talks like that.

dialogo.texto: Yo lo escucho todos los días en clase. Martina dice «querés» y yo digo «quieres», y nos entendemos muy bien. Pero quiero aprobar el examen y quiero estar segura de que reconozco todas las formas.

traduccion.en: I hear it every day in class. Martina says “querés” and I say “quieres,” and we understand each other very well. But I want to pass the exam and I want to be sure that I recognize all the forms.

dialogo.texto: Gracias. Quiero que todos entiendan algo importante. El voseo rioplatense no es un error: es una variedad correcta del español. En este módulo van a escucharlo muchas veces y también puede aparecer en el examen, así que deben reconocer esas formas y entender qué significan. Pero no tienen que usar el voseo. Emma puede seguir con tú, y a mí ustedes me hablan de usted.

traduccion.en: Thank you. I want everyone to understand something important. The River Plate voseo is not a mistake: it is a correct variety of Spanish. In this module you are going to hear it many times and it can also appear in the exam, so you must recognize these forms and understand what they mean. But you do not have to use the voseo. Emma can keep using tú, and with me you use usted.

dialogo.texto: Eso es. Yo te hablo de vos y vos me hablás de tú, y no hay ningún problema. Además, mi tonada no es tan difícil, ¿verdad, Emma?

traduccion.en: That's it. I talk to you with vos and you talk to me with tú, and there is no problem at all. Besides, my accent is not so hard, right, Emma?

dialogo.texto: Para nada. Profesora, entonces, cuando Martina dice «vos tenés», ¿yo debo entender «tú tienes»?

traduccion.en: Not at all. Teacher, so when Martina says “vos tenés,” should I understand “tú tienes”?

dialogo.texto: Exacto. Cuando dice «vení», debe entender «ven»; cuando dice «decime», «dime», y cuando dice «mirá», «mira». Para varias personas no hay diferencia: Martina dice «ustedes», como todos. Como tarea, cada uno va a escribir tres frases de Martina en forma de tú.

traduccion.en: Exactly. When she says “vení,” you should understand “ven”; when she says “decime,” “dime,” and when she says “mirá,” “mira.” For several people there is no difference: Martina says “ustedes,” like everyone else. As homework, each of you is going to write three of Martina's sentences in tú form.

dialogo.texto: Empiezo yo: «Mirá, vos sos muy amable y hablás muy bien español». Ahora escribí la frase en tú, Emma.

traduccion.en: I'll start: “Mirá, vos sos muy amable y hablás muy bien español.” Now write the sentence in tú, Emma.

dialogo.texto: A ver: «Mira, tú eres muy amable y hablas muy bien español.» La segunda: «¿Quieres un café?», que antes era «¿Querés un café?». Y la tercera: «Ven, siéntate aquí», que antes era «Vení, sentate acá».

traduccion.en: Let's see: “Mira, tú eres muy amable y hablas muy bien español.” The second one: “¿Quieres un café?”, which was “¿Querés un café?” before. And the third: “Ven, siéntate aquí,” which was “Vení, sentate acá” before.

dialogo.texto: Muy bien, Emma. Ahora lo contrario. Martina, yo digo una frase con tú y usted la dice con voseo: «¿Tienes tiempo?» y «¿Vives en Quito?».

traduccion.en: Very good, Emma. Now the opposite. Martina, I say a sentence with tú and you say it with voseo: “¿Tienes tiempo?” and “¿Vives en Quito?”

dialogo.texto: «¿Tenés tiempo?» y «¿Vivís en Quito?». Y «tú eres de Quito» es «vos sos de Quito»: ser es el único verbo irregular.

traduccion.en: “¿Tenés tiempo?” and “¿Vivís en Quito?” And “tú eres de Quito” is “vos sos de Quito”: ser is the only irregular verb.

dialogo.texto: Entonces tú eres, vos sos y usted es: tres formas de tratamiento para una sola persona.

traduccion.en: So tú eres, vos sos and usted es: three forms of address for a single person.

dialogo.texto: Exacto, y todas son correctas. Recuerden la tarea: tres frases de Martina en forma de tú. Y para varias personas, siempre ustedes.

traduccion.en: Exactly, and all of them are correct. Remember the homework: three of Martina's sentences in tú form. And for several people, always ustedes.

dialogo.texto: ¡Perfecto! Ya tenés tus tres frases. Después de la clase, ¿querés un café? Hay una máquina en el pasillo.

traduccion.en: Perfect! You already have your three sentences. After class, do you want a coffee? There is a machine in the hallway.

dialogo.texto: Sí, gracias. Quiero un café sin azúcar. Y gracias por tu ayuda con el voseo.

traduccion.en: Yes, thanks. I'd like a coffee without sugar. And thanks for your help with the voseo.

consigna.en: Where is Martina from?

feedback.en: Martina says: Soy de Buenos Aires, soy porteña.

consigna.en: What does Martina offer Emma?

feedback.en: Martina asks: ¿Querés un café? and mentions the machine in the hallway.

consigna.en: Choose the sentence that uses voseo.

feedback.en: Vos sos is the voseo. Tú eres uses tú and usted es uses usted.

consigna.en: Complete the tú version of «Vos querés un café».

feedback.en: Tú quieres: the tú form keeps the diphthong ie, while the vos form is querés.

consigna.en: Listen and choose what Martina asks.

feedback.en: Mirá, vení un momento: vení is the vos command of venir, so Martina asks the other person to come.

consigna.en: Rewrite in standard tú: «Vos tenés razón.»

feedback.en: Tú tienes razón: the vos form tenés becomes tienes.

titulo.en: Andean and Mexican expressions

objetivo.en: Recognize Andean and Mexican expressions (dame pasando, ¿mande?, ¡achachay!) and understand what they mean in standard Spanish.

traduccion.en: the mountain region, the highlands

nota.en: Say “seh-rrah-NEE-ah”: the rr is a trilled r and the stress falls on the í. It comes from sierra and means a stretch of mountains, here the Andes of Ecuador.

traduccion.en: the small village

nota.en: Say “ahl-DEH-ah”: the d is soft, like the th in “this”, and the stress falls on the e. An aldea is smaller than a pueblo.

traduccion.en: the bitter cold (literary or rural word)

nota.en: Say “eh-LOHR”: the h is silent and the stress falls on the last syllable. It is a strong word for el frío, often used in the countryside.

traduccion.en: the local guide who knows the land

nota.en: Say “bah-keh-AH-noh”: qu sounds like a k. The word is used in the Andes and in southern South America; you will also see baquiano. It is el baqueano for a man and la baqueana for a woman.

traduccion.en: the narrow path, the trail

nota.en: Say “TROH-chah”: ch sounds like the ch in “church” and the r is a single tap, like the tt in American “butter”. A trocha is a path that people have made by walking.

traduccion.en: to stretch out, to hold out

nota.en: Say “ehks-tehn-DEHR”: the stress falls on the last syllable. It changes e to ie in the present: extiendo, extiendes, extiende. Extender la mano is “to hold out your hand”.

traduccion.en: to give as a gift

nota.en: Say “rreh-gah-LAHR”: a word that starts with r has a trilled rr, and the g before a is a hard g, as in “go”. Les regalo un consejo means “I'll give you a piece of advice”, a friendly way to start a tip.

traduccion.en: the water bottle (for hiking)

nota.en: Say “kahn-teem-PLOH-rah”: the stress falls on the plo. A cantimplora is the bottle or flask that hikers carry to drink water on the trail.

traduccion.en: the seasoning mix

nota.en: Say “ah-LEE-nyoh”: ñ sounds like the ny in “canyon”. In Ecuador el aliño is the mix of seasonings, for example garlic, onion and cumin, that is used to flavor a soup or a meat.

explicacion.en: The highland pattern uses a gerund, not an infinitive. English speakers want an infinitive after “give me”, but here the form is dame + pasando.
Learners who know mande from a Mexican relative use it everywhere, even in Quito. It is a Mexican habit: in Ecuador people say ¿cómo? or ¿perdón? when they did not hear.
In English you “are cold”, so learners say estoy frío. Spanish uses tener: tengo frío. Estar frío describes a thing that is cold.

titulo.en: Expressions that come from a region

texto.en: Every region of the Spanish-speaking world has its own expressions. Three of them appear in this class. In the highlands of Ecuador, «dame pasando el agua» means «pásame el agua»: dar + gerund is a polite way to ask for a favor. In Mexico, «¿mande?» means «¿cómo?» or «¿perdón?» and people use it when they did not hear something. And «¡achachay!» is an Ecuadorian word of Quechua origin that means «¡qué frío!». These are cultural notes: you recognize them, you understand them and you can thank the person who uses them, but you do not have to use them yourself.

titulo.en: How dar + gerund works

texto.en: You already know the gerund (-ando, -iendo) from estar + gerund and from sentences like “vamos caminando”. In the highlands, the verb dar plus a gerund is a polite way to ask someone to do something for you: «dame pasando la sal», «me das cerrando la puerta». The gerund names the action and the thing you want comes after it. With usted it is «deme pasando…». If you hear it, translate it into the plain command: dame pasando = pásame. Do not try to use it with people from other regions: they may not understand it.

titulo.en: Three expressions and their standard version

texto.en: These expressions are cultural notes: you recognize them and understand them, but you do not have to use them.

apoyo.en: the highlands of Ecuador (a polite way to ask)

traduccion.en: Please pass me the water.

nota.en: In the Ecuadorian highlands dar + gerund is a polite request. In standard Spanish: Pásame el agua.

traduccion.en: Could you pass me the salt?

nota.en: The same pattern as a question, with tú: me das + gerund.

traduccion.en: Please close the door.

nota.en: It works with other verbs too: dame + gerund + the thing. Standard: Cierra la puerta, por favor.

items.texto: Deme pasando el pan, por favor.

traduccion.en: Please pass me the bread.

nota.en: With usted the pattern is deme + gerund.

traduccion.en: Brr! What bitter cold!

nota.en: Achachay is a word of Quechua origin that Ecuadorians use when they feel cold.

traduccion.en: Pardon? I didn't hear well.

nota.en: In Mexico people say mande when they did not hear something. It means ¿cómo?

items.texto: Mi abuelo decía «mande» cuando no oía bien.

traduccion.en: My grandfather used to say “mande” when he could not hear well.

nota.en: Decía and oía are imperfect forms: they describe a habit in the past.

items.texto: Les regalo un consejo: tomen agua de la cantimplora.

traduccion.en: I'll give you a piece of advice: drink water from your water bottle.

nota.en: Regalar un consejo is a friendly way to introduce a tip.

titulo.en: Dar + gerund: a polite request

texto.en: In the highlands of Ecuador you can ask for something by combining dar with the gerund of the action you want.

nota.en: dar in the imperative or in a question: tú, tú, usted
pasando, cerrando, esperando: the action you ask for
el agua, la puerta, un momento
in standard Spanish you use the plain command: pásame el agua

traduccion.en: Please pass me the scarf.

nota.en: Standard: Pásame la bufanda.

traduccion.en: Please wait for me a moment.

nota.en: Standard: Espérame un momento.

traduccion.en: Could you close the window?

nota.en: Standard: ¿Puedes cerrar la ventana?

feedback.en: Dame pasando el agua = Pásame el agua. The gerund names the action you ask for, and dame makes the request polite.

feedback.en: Mande = ¿cómo? or ¿perdón?: you ask the other person to repeat.

feedback.en: Dame pasando = pásame, ¿mande? = ¿cómo? and ¡achachay! = ¡qué frío!

feedback.en: ¡Achachay! means ¡qué frío!, so the speaker is cold, and dame pasando la bufanda means pásame la bufanda.

opciones: Tiene frío y pide la bufanda.

consigna.en: Put the pieces in order to write the standard version: “Pass me the water, please.”

feedback.en: Pásame el agua, por favor: the command pásame already includes me. Por favor can also go first.

contexto.en: Saturday, March 19, 2033. Emma García, Martina and Mateo Ruiz take a day trip to a village in the Ecuadorian highlands with a local Guía. The three friends use tú with each other (Martina with voseo) and usted with the Guía.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días y bienvenidos a la serranía. Yo soy baqueano: conozco cada trocha de estas montañas desde niño. Hoy vamos a subir caminando hasta una aldea pequeña y allá vamos a almorzar. Tengan cuidado, porque hoy hace mucho frío.

traduccion.en: Good morning and welcome to the highlands. I am a baqueano: I have known every trail in these mountains since I was a child. Today we are going to climb on foot to a small village and we are going to have lunch there. Be careful, because it is very cold today.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días, señor, y gracias por su ayuda. Emma, Martina, ¿ven esa aldea allá arriba? Se ve muy lejos.

traduccion.en: Good morning, sir, and thank you for your help. Emma, Martina, do you see that village up there? It looks very far.

dialogo.texto: ¡Achachay! Qué helor. A esta hora es normal, pero cuando salga el sol va a calentar. Mateo, dame pasando la bufanda gris que está en tu mochila, porque yo no traje la mía.

traduccion.en: Achachay! What bitter cold. At this hour it is normal, but when the sun comes out it will warm up. Mateo, pass me the gray scarf that is in your backpack, because I didn't bring mine.

dialogo.texto: ¿Mande? Con el viento no oí bien.

traduccion.en: Pardon? With the wind I didn't hear well.

dialogo.texto: A mí tampoco me quedó claro. ¿Qué quiere decir «dame pasando»? ¿Y qué es «achachay»? Emma, vos sabés más del español de acá, ¿no?

traduccion.en: It wasn't clear to me either. What does “dame pasando” mean? And what is “achachay”? Emma, you know more about the Spanish from here, right?

dialogo.texto: Un poco, lo aprendí aquí en Ecuador. En la sierra, «dame pasando la bufanda» significa «pásame la bufanda», pero se dice con más cortesía. Y «¡achachay!» significa «¡qué frío!». Es una palabra de origen quechua.

traduccion.en: A little, I learned it here in Ecuador. In the highlands, “dame pasando la bufanda” means “pásame la bufanda,” but it is said more politely. And “¡achachay!” means “¡qué frío!” It is a word of Quechua origin.

dialogo.texto: Y yo dije «mande» porque soy mexicano: significa «¿cómo?» o «¿perdón?». Es lo que digo cuando no oí bien lo que alguien dijo. Mi mamá lo decía mucho en Guadalajara.

traduccion.en: And I said “mande” because I am Mexican: it means “¿cómo?” or “¿perdón?” It is what I say when I didn't hear well what someone said. My mom said it a lot in Guadalajara.

dialogo.texto: ¡Mi abuelo también lo decía! Era de Guadalajara y, aunque en casa solo hablábamos inglés, siempre decía «mande» cuando no oía bien.

traduccion.en: My grandfather used to say it too! He was from Guadalajara and, although we only spoke English at home, he always said “mande” when he could not hear well.

dialogo.texto: Aquí tiene la bufanda, señor.

traduccion.en: Here is the scarf, sir.

dialogo.texto: Mirá, Mateo le extiende la bufanda al guía con las dos manos. Qué atento. Yo siempre llevo cantimplora, pero hoy la dejé en mi departamento.

traduccion.en: Look, Mateo is holding out the scarf to the guide with both hands. How considerate. I always carry a water bottle, but today I left it at my apartment.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, joven. Les regalo un consejo: en la trocha caminen despacio y tomen agua de la cantimplora. Y si algo no entienden, me preguntan: en la sierra usamos palabras que no están en los libros.

traduccion.en: Thank you, young man. I'll give you a piece of advice: on the trail walk slowly and drink water from your water bottle. And if you do not understand something, ask me: in the highlands we use words that are not in the books.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, señor. Una pregunta más: ¿qué es exactamente un baqueano?

traduccion.en: Thank you, sir. One more question: what exactly is a baqueano?

dialogo.texto: Es el guía que conoce la tierra: sabe dónde está cada trocha, dónde hay agua y cuándo viene la lluvia. Mi abuelo era baqueano y yo aprendí de él. La aldea tiene unas cuarenta casas y una iglesia pequeña.

traduccion.en: He is the guide who knows the land: he knows where each trail is, where there is water and when the rain comes. My grandfather was a baqueano and I learned from him. The village has about forty houses and a small church.

dialogo.texto: Qué bonito. Otra cosa, señor: en la aldea, ¿podemos comer algo caliente? Con este helor, necesito una sopa.

traduccion.en: How nice. Another thing, sir: in the village, can we eat something hot? With this bitter cold, I need a soup.

dialogo.texto: Claro que sí. En la aldea hay una señora que prepara una sopa de papas con aliño de ajo y cebolla. Cuando llegamos, ella siempre dice «¡dame pasando los platos!» y todos ayudamos. Una cosa más sobre «achachay»: los niños de la aldea lo dicen cuando entran al agua del río, porque está muy fría. Para ellos es un juego.

traduccion.en: Of course. In the village there is a lady who makes a potato soup with a seasoning mix of garlic and onion. When we arrive, she always says “¡dame pasando los platos!” and we all help. One more thing about “achachay”: the children of the village say it when they go into the river water, because it is very cold. For them it is a game.

dialogo.texto: Perfecto. Estoy escribiendo tres cosas para el examen: «dame pasando» es «pásame», «¿mande?» es «¿cómo?» y «achachay» es «qué frío». Son notas culturales: las entiendo, pero no tengo que decir esas palabras.

traduccion.en: Perfect. I am writing down three things for the exam: “dame pasando” is “pásame,” “¿mande?” is “¿cómo?” and “achachay” is “qué frío.” They are cultural notes: I understand them, but I do not have to say those words.

dialogo.texto: Yo sí voy a decir «achachay»: me encanta. ¡Achachay! Mejor empecemos a caminar antes de que tengamos más frío.

traduccion.en: I am going to say “achachay”: I love it. Achachay! Let's start walking before we get any colder.

dialogo.texto: Muy bien, jóvenes. Sigan la trocha y yo voy adelante. En una hora llegamos a la aldea.

traduccion.en: Very good, young people. Follow the trail and I'll go ahead. In an hour we reach the village.

titulo.en: Casa, caza and the Spanish z

objetivo.en: Recognize the z/ce/ci distinction versus seseo when you listen to a speaker from Spain, and explain the difference.

traduccion.en: the pronunciation

nota.en: Say “proh-noon-syah-SYOHN”: c before i sounds like an s in Latin America (like a th in most of Spain), and the stress falls on the last syllable.

traduccion.en: the interdental sound (the Spanish th sound)

nota.en: Say “een-tehr-dehn-TAHL”: the stress falls on the last syllable. Interdental means “between the teeth”: you put the tip of your tongue between your teeth, as for the th in “think”. Here la interdental is the consonant sound of the Spanish z in Spain.

traduccion.en: the seseo (pronouncing z, ce and ci as s)

nota.en: Say “seh-SEH-oh”: the stress falls on the second syllable. El seseo is the normal pronunciation in Latin America, in the Canary Islands and in the south of Spain: z, ce and ci sound like an s.

traduccion.en: house, home

nota.en: Say “KAH-sah”: the same in Ecuador and in Spain. Casa is spelled with s, so the sound is an s everywhere.

traduccion.en: hunting

nota.en: In Ecuador it sounds exactly like casa: “KAH-sah”. In most of Spain the z is interdental: “KAH-thah”. The spelling is the only clue in Ecuador.

traduccion.en: to sew

nota.en: Say “koh-SEHR”: the r at the end is a single tap, like the tt in American “butter”. In Ecuador it sounds the same as cocer.

traduccion.en: to cook in boiling water, to boil

nota.en: In Ecuador it sounds like coser: “koh-SEHR”. In most of Spain the c is interdental: “koh-THEHR”. It changes o to ue in the present: cuece, cuecen.

traduccion.en: the sky

nota.en: Say “SYEH-loh” in Ecuador; in most of Spain the first sound is interdental: “THYEH-loh”. Ci is written with c, but the sound is an s in Latin America.

traduccion.en: they sound the same

nota.en: Say “SWEH-nahn ee-GWAHL”. Sonar changes o to ue (suena, suenan). Casa y caza suenan igual en Ecuador. The opposite is suenan distinto.

Learners who hear a speaker from Spain copy sois, even in Quito. In Ecuador and the rest of Latin America the plural “you” is ustedes + son.

titulo.en: Two ways of pronouncing z, ce and ci

texto.en: In most of Spain, z, ce and ci sound like the th of English “think”: zapato, cielo, gracias. This sound is called interdental because the tongue goes between the teeth. In Latin America, and also in the south of Spain, z, ce and ci sound like an s: this is the seseo. So in Ecuador casa and caza sound the same, and so do coser and cocer; in most of Spain they sound different. The seseo is correct, it is the pronunciation you learned in Quito, and the spelling is the same everywhere. This class is a recognition note: you do not have to change your pronunciation, but you must understand a speaker who has the interdental.

titulo.en: What to listen for

texto.en: When a speaker from Spain says zapato, cena, cinco or gracias, you will hear the interdental where an Ecuadorian hears an s. Do not be confused: casa is spelled with s, so it sounds the same in both systems; only the words with z, ce and ci change. In the DELE C1 listening tasks you will hear speakers from several regions, so you should recognize both pronunciations and the other signs of Spain, such as vosotros: ¿cuántas sois? means ¿cuántas son ustedes?

contexto.en: Tuesday, March 22, 2033. Emma García and Martina call a hotel in Madrid that Daniela Andrade recommended for a vacation trip they are planning for July (the trip itself is not shown). Quito is six hours behind Madrid, so it is still morning for them. The Recepcionista is from Spain; Emma and Martina use usted with her and tú with each other (Martina with voseo).

dialogo.texto: Hotel, buenas tardes. ¿Dígame?

traduccion.en: Hotel, good afternoon. How can I help you?

dialogo.texto: Buenas tardes. Llamamos desde Quito, en Ecuador: aquí todavía es de mañana. Una amiga, Daniela Andrade, nos habló de su hotel y queremos reservar una habitación para las vacaciones de julio.

traduccion.en: Good afternoon. We are calling from Quito, in Ecuador: here it is still morning. A friend, Daniela Andrade, told us about your hotel and we would like to book a room for the July vacation.

dialogo.texto: Muchas gracias por llamar. ¿Para cuántas noches? ¿Y cuántas sois?

traduccion.en: Thank you very much for calling. For how many nights? And how many of you are there?

dialogo.texto: Somos dos, mi amiga y yo, y queremos cuatro noches, con desayuno. ¿Cuánto cuesta una habitación doble?

traduccion.en: There are two of us, my friend and I, and we would like four nights, with breakfast. How much is a double room?

dialogo.texto: La doble cuesta ochenta euros la noche, con desayuno. El desayuno es de siete a diez, y también hay cena: son veinte euros por persona. Estamos a cinco minutos del centro y desde la terraza se ve el cielo de Madrid. Es una vista preciosa. En julio tenemos habitaciones libres, pero hay mucha gente: es mejor reservar pronto.

traduccion.en: The double room costs eighty euros a night, with breakfast. Breakfast is from seven to ten, and there is also dinner: it is twenty euros per person. We are five minutes from downtown and from the terrace you can see the Madrid sky. It is a beautiful view. In July we have rooms available, but there are many people: it is better to book soon.

dialogo.texto: Perfecto, nos parece bien. Voy a hablar con mi amiga y le confirmo por correo hoy o mañana. Muchas gracias por su ayuda.

traduccion.en: Perfect, that sounds good to us. I am going to talk with my friend and I will confirm by email today or tomorrow. Thank you very much for your help.

dialogo.texto: De nada. Hasta pronto y buen día.

traduccion.en: You're welcome. See you soon and have a good day.

dialogo.texto: Emma, ¿notaste cómo dijo «gracias», «cinco» y «cena»? Con la interdental, con la lengua entre los dientes, como la th del inglés. Yo digo esas palabras con s.

traduccion.en: Emma, did you notice how she said “gracias,” “cinco” and “cena”? With the interdental, with the tongue between the teeth, like the English th. I say those words with an s.

dialogo.texto: Claro que lo noté. En gran parte de España, z, ce y ci suenan con la interdental. En Ecuador, en Argentina y en el resto de Latinoamérica tenemos seseo: suenan como una s. La ortografía es la misma; solo cambia la pronunciación.

traduccion.en: Of course I noticed. In a large part of Spain, z, ce and ci sound with the interdental. In Ecuador, in Argentina and in the rest of Latin America we have seseo: they sound like an s. The spelling is the same; only the pronunciation changes.

dialogo.texto: O sea que mi pronunciación no es un error, es seseo, ¿no? Igual que mi voseo. Pero ¿todos en España hablan con la interdental, o solo en Madrid?

traduccion.en: So my pronunciation is not a mistake, it is seseo, right? Just like my voseo. But does everyone in Spain speak with the interdental, or only in Madrid?

dialogo.texto: No, no todos. En el sur de España también hay seseo, y la interdental es más del centro y del norte. Y fíjate en otra cosa: la recepcionista dijo «¿cuántas sois?». Esa es la forma de vosotras, que solo se usa en España. Nosotras decimos «¿cuántas son ustedes?».

traduccion.en: No, not everyone. In the south of Spain there is also seseo, and the interdental is more from the center and the north. And notice something else: the receptionist said “¿cuántas sois?” That is the vosotras form, which is only used in Spain. We say “¿cuántas son ustedes?”

dialogo.texto: Entiendo. Pero decime algo: si ella dice distinto la z y la s, ¿«casa» y «caza» suenan distinto para ella?

traduccion.en: I understand. But tell me something: if she says the z and the s differently, do “casa” and “caza” sound different to her?

dialogo.texto: Sí. En España «casa» y «caza» no suenan igual, porque «caza» tiene la interdental. En Ecuador suenan igual. Y pasa lo mismo con «coser» y «cocer»: aquí suenan igual, pero en España no.

traduccion.en: Yes. In Spain “casa” and “caza” do not sound the same, because “caza” has the interdental. In Ecuador they sound the same. And the same happens with “coser” and “cocer”: here they sound the same, but in Spain they do not.

dialogo.texto: Qué curioso. Para una persona de Madrid no son la misma palabra, y para mí sí. Voy a escribir eso para el examen. Una última pregunta: ¿por qué Daniela nos habló de ese hotel y no de otro?

traduccion.en: How curious. For a person from Madrid they are not the same word, and for me they are. I am going to write it down for the exam. One last question: why did Daniela tell us about that hotel and not another?

dialogo.texto: Porque tiene una terraza con una vista preciosa y la habitación no cuesta mucho. Y en julio vamos a escuchar el español de España en la calle.

traduccion.en: Because it has a terrace with a beautiful view and the room doesn't cost much. And in July we are going to hear the Spanish of Spain on the street.

dialogo.texto: Buena idea. Entonces voy a escuchar con atención: en el examen puede aparecer una voz de España.

traduccion.en: Good idea. Then I am going to listen carefully: in the exam a voice from Spain may appear.

dialogo.texto: Exacto. Es una nota de pronunciación: no tienes que hablar como en España, solo reconocer la diferencia. Y ahora, a escribir el correo para confirmar el hotel.

traduccion.en: Exactly. It is a pronunciation note: you do not have to speak like in Spain, only recognize the difference. And now, let's write the email to confirm the hotel.

nota.en: Say “frah-SAH-dah”: the z sounds like an s and the d between vowels is soft, like the th in “this”. It is used in Argentina, Uruguay and the Andes. In Spain: la manta.

nota.en: Say “eh-lah-DEH-rah”: the h is silent and the d is soft. It is used in Argentina and Uruguay. In Spain: la nevera.

nota.en: Say “KOH-cheh”: ch sounds like the ch in “church”. In Spain it is the normal word for the car; in Ecuador you say el carro.

nota.en: Say “MOH-beel”: the stress falls on the first syllable, which is why it has an accent mark, and the v sounds like a b. In Latin America: el celular.

traduccion.en: the computer (Spain)

nota.en: Say “ohr-deh-nah-DOHR”: the stress falls on the last syllable. In Latin America: la computadora.

traduccion.en: the juice (Spain)

nota.en: Say “SOO-moh” in Latin America; in most of Spain the z is interdental: “THOO-moh”. In Latin America: el jugo.

traduccion.en: the apartment (Spain)

nota.en: Say “PEE-soh”. In Spain it is the normal word for an apartment. In Ecuador, el piso is the floor of a building (el segundo piso) or the surface you walk on; the apartment is el departamento.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Voy a manejar mi carro al trabajo.

explicacion.en: Textbooks from Spain teach conducir and coche, and both are correct there. In Ecuador people say manejar and carro, and this course practices the Latin American words.
Billete is the word for ticket in Spain. In Ecuador a billete is a bill of money, so a clerk may think you want to exchange money. For a ticket say boleto.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Vivo en un piso en Quito.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Vivo en un departamento en Quito.

explicacion.en: Learners who heard piso from a speaker of Spain use it in Ecuador. There, piso means the floor of a building or the surface you walk on; the place where you live is el departamento.

titulo.en: Two words for one thing

texto.en: Spanish is spoken in more than twenty countries, and the vocabulary changes from one region to another. A car is un carro in Ecuador and un coche in Spain; a cell phone is un celular in Latin America and un móvil in Spain; a computer is una computadora or un ordenador. Neither word is wrong: each one is correct in its region. In this course you produce the Latin American vocabulary, because you live in Quito, and you recognize the words from Spain, because you will meet speakers from Spain and texts from Spain in the DELE C1.

titulo.en: How to learn the pairs

texto.en: Learn each pair as one concept with two words: carro / coche, jugo / zumo, departamento / piso. Some words also exist in both places with different meanings: in Ecuador piso is a floor of a building and billete is a bill of money, so a mix-up can be funny. There are more pairs to recognize and use: la frazada (América) / la manta (España); el durazno / el melocotón; la frutilla / la fresa; la heladera / la nevera. When someone uses a word you do not know, ask what it means, and then use the Latin American one.

contexto.en: Thursday, March 24, 2033, at the Instituto Andino de Idiomas. A new classmate from Madrid joins the DELE C1 course as a listener. Emma García, Martina and the Compañero use tú with one another; Martina speaks with voseo. The Compañero speaks with the vocabulary of Spain (you only recognize it), and Emma answers with the Latin American vocabulary she learned in Ecuador.

dialogo.texto: Buenas tardes. Soy nuevo en el curso y vengo de España. ¿Me puedo sentar aquí?

traduccion.en: Good afternoon. I am new to the course and I come from Spain. May I sit here?

dialogo.texto: Claro, siéntate. Yo soy Emma y ella es Martina. Bienvenido al curso. ¿De qué parte de España eres?

traduccion.en: Of course, sit down. I'm Emma and she is Martina. Welcome to the course. What part of Spain are you from?

dialogo.texto: Vengo de Madrid. Llegué hace dos días a Quito y vivo en un piso cerca del instituto.

traduccion.en: I come from Madrid. I arrived in Quito two days ago and I live in a piso near the institute.

dialogo.texto: ¿En un piso? Para mí «piso» es el nivel de un edificio. ¿Te referís a un departamento?

traduccion.en: In a piso? For me “piso” is a floor of a building. Do you mean an apartment?

dialogo.texto: Claro, un departamento, como se dice aquí. Qué lío: ya no sé qué palabra usar.

traduccion.en: Of course, a departamento, as people say here. What a mess: I no longer know which word to use.

dialogo.texto: Es normal. Yo aprendí el español de Ecuador, así que digo «departamento», «carro», «celular», «computadora» y «jugo». Tú, en cambio, dices «piso», «coche», «móvil», «ordenador» y «zumo».

traduccion.en: That's normal. I learned Ecuadorian Spanish, so I say “departamento,” “carro,” “celular,” “computadora” and “jugo.” You, on the other hand, say “piso,” “coche,” “móvil,” “ordenador” and “zumo.”

dialogo.texto: Exacto, y las dos listas están bien. Esta mañana pedí un zumo de naranja y la mesera me trajo un jugo. Sabe igual, pero me costó entender que era lo mismo. Y hay otra cosa que me pasó ayer: en la terminal pedí un billete para el autobús y el empleado me preguntó si quería cambiar dinero.

traduccion.en: Exactly, and both lists are fine. This morning I asked for a zumo de naranja and the waitress brought me a jugo. It tastes the same, but it took me a while to understand that it was the same thing. And something else happened to me yesterday: at the terminal I asked for a billete for the bus and the clerk asked me whether I wanted to exchange money.

dialogo.texto: Claro, aquí un «billete» es un billete de dinero. El papel para viajar se llama «boleto»: un boleto de autobús, un boleto de avión.

traduccion.en: Of course, here a “billete” is a bill of money. The paper you need for a trip is called a “boleto”: a bus ticket, a plane ticket.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y por qué viniste a Quito? Yo vine por mi trabajo.

traduccion.en: And why did you come to Quito? I came for my job.

dialogo.texto: Doy clases de español en Madrid y quiero ver cómo se prepara el DELE C1 en este curso. Me interesa mucho el español de aquí.

traduccion.en: I teach Spanish in Madrid and I want to see how the DELE C1 is prepared for in this course. I am very interested in the Spanish from here.

dialogo.texto: Qué casualidad: yo también doy clases aquí, de inglés, y trabajo en turismo comunitario. Seguro que vas a escuchar muchas palabras nuevas.

traduccion.en: What a coincidence: I teach here too, English, and I work in community tourism. I'm sure you will hear many new words.

dialogo.texto: Entonces no es un error, es otra variedad. Me gusta: dos palabras para una cosa. Yo digo «frazada», «durazno», «frutilla» y «heladera», y vos decís «manta», «melocotón», «fresa» y «nevera», ¿no?

traduccion.en: So it is not a mistake, it is another variety. I like it: two words for one thing. I say “frazada,” “durazno,” “frutilla” and “heladera,” and you say “manta,” “melocotón,” “fresa” and “nevera,” right?

dialogo.texto: Eso es. Y con los verbos pasa lo mismo: en España conducimos el coche y aquí ustedes manejan el carro.

traduccion.en: That's it. And the same happens with verbs: in Spain we drive the coche and here you drive the carro.

dialogo.texto: Por eso aquí digo «manejo mi carro» y tú dices «conduzco mi coche». Para el DELE C1 las dos formas están bien, pero en el curso practicamos las palabras de Latinoamérica.

traduccion.en: That's why here I say “manejo mi carro” and you say “conduzco mi coche.” For the DELE C1 both forms are fine, but in the course we practice the words from Latin America.

dialogo.texto: Hagamos una lista de pares para estudiar. Escribí vos, Emma, la columna de Latinoamérica, y el compañero escribe la de España.

traduccion.en: Let's make a list of pairs to study. You write the Latin American column, Emma, and our classmate writes the one for Spain.

dialogo.texto: Ya está: carro y coche, celular y móvil, computadora y ordenador, jugo y zumo, departamento y piso, boleto y billete. Y los pares de Martina: frazada y manta, durazno y melocotón, frutilla y fresa, heladera y nevera.

traduccion.en: Done: carro and coche, celular and móvil, computadora and ordenador, jugo and zumo, departamento and piso, boleto and billete. And Martina's pairs: frazada and manta, durazno and melocotón, frutilla and fresa, heladera and nevera.

dialogo.texto: Aprendo más en esta lista que en un mes de clases. Para el curso voy a usar las palabras de aquí, aunque en España voy a seguir diciendo «ordenador».

traduccion.en: I am learning more with this list than in a month of classes. For the course I am going to use the words from here, although in Spain I am going to keep saying “ordenador.”

dialogo.texto: En mi departamento tengo una frazada, una computadora y una heladera: tres palabras de mi lista.

traduccion.en: In my apartment I have a frazada, a computadora and a heladera: three words from my list.

dialogo.texto: En mi piso, o sea, en mi departamento, tengo un ordenador, una nevera y una manta: las mismas cosas con otros nombres.

traduccion.en: In my piso, I mean, in my departamento, I have an ordenador, a nevera and a manta: the same things with other names.

dialogo.texto: Perfecto. Y si alguien dice una palabra que no conoces, solo pregunta. Así aprendemos todos.

traduccion.en: Perfect. And if someone says a word you do not know, just ask. That way we all learn.

titulo.en: ¿Cómo se dice aquí…? Negotiating meaning

objetivo.en: Negotiate the meaning of a word with someone who speaks another variety: ask how something is said here, what it means and whether it is used the same way.

traduccion.en: the meaning

nota.en: Say “seeg-nee-fee-KAH-doh”: the g is a hard g, as in “go”, and the d between vowels is soft, like the th in “this”. ¿Cuál es el significado de…? asks for the meaning of a word.

traduccion.en: the expression, the phrase

nota.en: Say “ehks-preh-SYOHN”: the stress falls on the last syllable. La expresión can be a word or a group of words that people use.

traduccion.en: the equivalent

nota.en: Say “eh-kee-vah-LEHN-teh”: qu sounds like a k and the v sounds like a b. It is the word that means the same in another place: el equivalente de pochoclo es canguil.

traduccion.en: the variant

nota.en: Say “bah-RYAHN-teh”: the v sounds like a b. A variante is another form of a word or expression that people use in a different region.

traduccion.en: the localism (a word used in one place)

nota.en: Say “loh-kah-LEES-moh”: the stress falls on the lis. A localismo is a word that people only use in one place or region.

traduccion.en: to use (a word, a tool)

nota.en: Say “ehm-pleh-AHR”: the stress falls on the last syllable. Emplear una palabra is a more formal way to say usar una palabra: Cada región emplea sus palabras.

traduccion.en: the sense, the meaning of a word (in the dictionary)

nota.en: Say “ah-sehp-SYOHN”: the c before e sounds like an s (like a th in most of Spain). One word can have several acepciones, the numbered meanings in a dictionary.

traduccion.en: it is said, people say

nota.en: Say “seh DEE-seh”: the d of dice is a hard d, as in “dog”, because it comes right after the s sound. ¿Cómo se dice…? asks how something is said, without naming anyone.

traduccion.en: the popcorn (Ecuador)

nota.en: Say “kahn-GEEL”: the stress falls on the last syllable and the g is a hard g, as in “go”. El canguil is the word for popcorn in Ecuador; Argentina says pochoclo and Spain says palomitas.

explicacion.en: English says “How do you say…?”, so learners translate it with dices. Spanish uses the impersonal se: ¿Cómo se dice…?
English says “What is the meaning of…?”, so learners translate it with qué es. Spanish uses cuál with significado, or the verb: ¿Qué significa…?
English “do you use it…?” can mean people in general, so learners use tú. Spanish asks about the people of the place with ustedes: ¿Lo usan…?

titulo.en: Asking about words

texto.en: When you talk with someone from another region, you will often meet a word that you do not know or that means something different. You can negotiate its meaning with four moves. First, ask for the local word: «¿Cómo se dice aquí «pochoclo»?». Second, ask for the meaning: «¿Qué quiere decir «canguil»?» or «¿Qué significa…?». Third, explain your own usage and ask if it is the same: «En Argentina se dice…; ¿lo usan igual aquí?». Fourth, confirm what you understood: «O sea que aquí se dice…». These moves keep a conversation going when varieties meet and avoid misunderstandings.

titulo.en: Useful words for talking about words

texto.en: To talk about words you need a small vocabulary: el significado (the meaning), la expresión, el equivalente (the same thing in another place), la variante, el localismo (a word used only in one place), emplear (to use) and la acepción (one meaning of a word). Remember that se dice is impersonal: do not say ¿Cómo dices…? when you mean “how do people say…?”. And remember that when you ask whether a place uses a word, you ask about the people there with ustedes: ¿lo usan igual aquí? If the other person is not sure, they can say «No sabría decirle».

contexto.en: Saturday, April 2, 2033, at the market of a highland town. Emma García and Martina talk with a local Vendedora. Emma and Martina use tú with each other (Martina with voseo) and usted with the Vendedora.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días, jóvenes. Pasen, pasen. Tengo choclo con queso, papas y canguil caliente.

traduccion.en: Good morning, young ladies. Come in, come in. I have corn on the cob with cheese, potatoes and hot popcorn.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días, señora. Qué rico huele. Perdone, ¿cómo se dice aquí «pochoclo»? En Argentina decimos «pochoclo», y es lo que se come en el cine.

traduccion.en: Good morning, ma'am. It smells so good. Excuse me, how do you say “pochoclo” here? In Argentina we say “pochoclo,” and it is what you eat at the movies.

dialogo.texto: Aquí eso se llama «canguil». En otros países le dicen «palomitas», pero en la sierra todos decimos «canguil».

traduccion.en: Here that is called “canguil.” In other countries they call it “palomitas,” but in the highlands we all say “canguil.”

dialogo.texto: O sea que aquí se dice «canguil» y en otros países, «palomitas». Qué interesante: cada país usa una expresión para la misma cosa.

traduccion.en: So here people say “canguil” and in other countries, “palomitas.” How interesting: each country has its own expression for the same thing.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y usted, joven, de dónde es? Habla muy bien, pero se nota que no es de aquí.

traduccion.en: And you, miss, where are you from? You speak very well, but you can tell you are not from here.

dialogo.texto: Soy de Chicago, pero vivo en Quito desde hace más de seis años. Aprendí español aquí y todavía aprendo palabras nuevas. Perdone, señora, tengo otra pregunta. Usted dijo «choclo con queso». Yo conozco «choclo», pero me gustaría saber qué quiere decir exactamente aquí. ¿Lo usan igual en todo el país?

traduccion.en: I am from Chicago, but I have lived in Quito for more than six years. I learned Spanish here and I still discover new words. Excuse me, ma'am, I have another question. You said “choclo con queso.” I know “choclo,” but I would like to know what it means exactly here. Do you use it the same way across the whole country?

dialogo.texto: Aquí «choclo» es el maíz tierno, todavía en la mazorca. No sabría decirle si en todo el país lo usan igual: yo solo conozco cómo lo decimos en mi pueblo. Es un localismo, creo, y quizá en otras regiones digan otra cosa.

traduccion.en: Here “choclo” is tender corn, still on the cob. I couldn't tell you whether they use it the same way across the whole country: I only know how we say it in my town. It is a localism, I think, and maybe in other regions they say something else.

dialogo.texto: O sea que «choclo» es el maíz tierno en la mazorca, y quizá hay otra variante en otras regiones. Muchas gracias.

traduccion.en: So “choclo” is tender corn on the cob, and maybe there is another variant in other regions. Thank you very much.

dialogo.texto: En Argentina «choclo» significa lo mismo, y «pochoclo» es el maíz que se revienta con el calor. Una palabra puede tener otra acepción en otro país, por eso conviene preguntar.

traduccion.en: In Argentina “choclo” means the same, and “pochoclo” is the corn that pops with heat. A word can have another sense in another country, so it is good to ask.

dialogo.texto: Así es, joven. Cada región puede emplear sus palabras, y todas están bien. Yo trabajo aquí en el mercado y los turistas me piden pochoclo, palomitas y otros nombres, y yo les entiendo a todos. Mi hija vivió en otro país y volvió con palabras que yo no conocía. Ahora ella me explica sus palabras y yo le explico las mías.

traduccion.en: That's right, miss. Each region can use its words, and all of them are fine. I work here at the market and the tourists ask me for pochoclo, palomitas and other names, and I understand all of them. My daughter lived in another country and came back with words that I did not know. Now she explains her words to me and I explain mine to her.

dialogo.texto: Esa es la mejor manera de aprender: preguntar qué quiere decir cada palabra y comprobar con «o sea que…».

traduccion.en: That is the best way to learn: ask what each word means and check with “o sea que…”.

dialogo.texto: Y a veces el equivalente exacto no existe, por eso conviene preguntar cómo se usa cada palabra en cada lugar. Una duda más, señora: ¿cómo se dice aquí «celular»? ¿Lo usan igual? Y la «frutilla», ¿también es «frutilla» aquí?

traduccion.en: And sometimes the exact equivalent does not exist, so it is good to ask how each word is used in each place. One more question, ma'am: how do you say “celular” here? Do you use it the same way? And “frutilla,” is it also “frutilla” here?

dialogo.texto: Sí, aquí también se dice «celular» y «frutilla». En España dicen «móvil» y «fresa», según me contó un cliente.

traduccion.en: Yes, here it is also “celular” and “frutilla.” In Spain they say “móvil” and “fresa,” according to a customer who told me.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, señora. Voy a escribir una lista: «canguil», «pochoclo» y «palomitas» para el maíz que se revienta, y «choclo» para el maíz tierno. ¿Me da una bolsa de canguil?

traduccion.en: Thank you, ma'am. I am going to write a list: “canguil,” “pochoclo” and “palomitas” for the corn that pops, and “choclo” for tender corn. Could I have a bag of popcorn?

dialogo.texto: Con mucho gusto. Son dos dólares. Cada día un turista me enseña una palabra nueva, y hoy fueron ustedes. Vuelvan cuando quieran, que aquí siempre les explico las palabras.

traduccion.en: My pleasure. That is two dollars. Every day a tourist teaches me a new word, and today it was you. Come back whenever you like, because here I will always explain the words to you.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, señora. Una misma cosa puede tener tres nombres, y hoy aprendí dos más. Voy a volver a este pueblo para probar el choclo con queso.

traduccion.en: Thank you, ma'am. One thing can have three names, and today I learned two more. I am going to come back to this town to try the choclo with cheese.
